coverage_gaps: Need updated public-company market caps, liquidity, short interest, analyst coverage, and valuation multiples for all candidates before Layer 2 ranking.
Need primary-source filings for every retained candidate; many Layer 1C names beyond the cached node evidence are hypotheses requiring 10-K/20-F/annual-report validation.
Need revenue materiality by education segment, especially for diversified companies such as Nelnet, Graham Holdings, Pearson, Wiley, Bright Horizons, and Extreme Networks.

Need clearer mapping of private but important education infrastructure vendors such as LMS, proctoring, student information systems, test delivery, credential verification, and university program managers; public proxies may be incomplete.
Need explicit separation between regulatory tailwinds and regulatory risk for Title IV institutions, student-loan servicers, virtual charter schools, and international tutoring operators.
Need employer-partnership validation for vocational names: partnerships must be tested against student starts, placement rates, completion rates, pricing, and margins.
Need education supplier-customer graph work using sources such as Scrutica, filings, and contract databases to identify hidden vendors behind visible operators.
Need K-12 public procurement, E-Rate, state virtual-school authorization, and district-contract evidence to validate network, curriculum, software, and school-improvement suppliers.
Need falsification triggers for AI disruption: study tools, content libraries, tutoring, language learning, and corporate training may face margin pressure if AI commoditizes course content.
Need non-U.S. regulatory review for TAL, EDU, AFYA, Laureate, and other international education names before comparing them with U.S. operators.

memory_update.text: Education Layer 1 universe should be split into visible reference leaders and a separate underfollowed lane of vocational operators, servicing/payment infrastructure, credentialing gates, K-12 workflow suppliers, LMS/software vendors, and education-adjacent employer-benefit platforms.

Student-loan servicing, school payment plans, SIS/enrollment workflows, communications, collections, and compliance software appear to be among the most promising underfollowed infrastructure nodes because they are regulated, sticky, and partially visible in Nelnet segment disclosures.

Employer-aligned vocational and healthcare training should remain a priority lane because bottlenecks may be physical capacity, labs, instructors, employer recognition, credential pass rates, and placement relationships rather than generic software.
Assessment, licensure, certification, and professional continuing education deserve separate tracking because these gates can capture value even if course content becomes commoditized by AI.

Layer 2 should verify revenue materiality and primary filings for all hypothesis names, with special scrutiny for Title IV, charter authorization, student-loan servicing contracts, international education regulation, and AI disruption risk.

The current universe is U.S.-heavy and public-company constrained; the next research pass should map private infrastructure vendors and then find public suppliers, owners, customers, or comparable proxies.

summary: Layer 1C merged the Education theme universe across visible demand anchors, regulated education operators, vocational/workforce training capacity, student-loan and education-payment infrastructure, K-12/district suppliers, assessment/credentialing gates, corporate-learning software, and speculative shadow suppliers. The highest Serenity relevance is not limited to consumer edtech brands; the stronger funnel emphasizes regulated workflows, accreditation/authorization, employer-recognized credentials, loan/payment rails, school administration software, curriculum/outcomes constraints, and second-order infrastructure vendors. This is a research-priority universe only, not a trading recommendation.
universe_method: multi-step: theme decomposition -> node expansion -> dedupe/rank
